course: Daily Pig Sales: Batch Farrowing System

lessons.title: Startup Costs Breakdown
lessons.body: Before you buy your first pig, you need to know exactly what you'll spend. In Africa, a small batch farrowing unit for 5 sows can start with about $3,000 to $5,000. The biggest costs are housing, equipment, and your first set of breeding stock. For housing, a simple open-sided shed with concrete floor and iron sheet roof costs around $1,500 for 5 sows and their piglets. You can reduce this by using local materials like bamboo and thatch, but concrete is better for cleaning and disease control. Equipment includes feeders, drinkers, and farrowing crates. A basic farrowing crate costs $80 to $120 each. You need at least 5 crates, so budget $500. Feeders and drinkers for 5 sows and 50 piglets cost about $300. A water tank and pipes: $200. Now breeding stock: a good young boar costs $200 to $400, and each sow costs $150 to $300. For 5 sows and 1 boar, that's roughly $1,000 to $1,900. Don't forget initial feed: you need to feed your pigs for at least 2 months before any sales. That's about 500 kg of feed at $0.50 per kg, so $250. Vet and vaccines for the first 3 months: $150. Labour: if you do it yourself, you save, but if you hire a caretaker, budget $100 per month. Transport for buying pigs and feed: $100. Miscellaneous (tools, buckets, disinfectants): $200. Total startup: about $4,000 to $5,000. To reduce costs, start small: 2 sows and 1 boar, use second-hand materials, and build slowly. But never compromise on concrete floors and proper drainageâthey save you money on disease treatment later. Write every expense down in a notebook. This is your baseline. Many farmers fail because they underestimate startup costs. Be honest with yourself. If you have $2,000, start with 2 sows. You can expand later from your profits.

lessons.title: Monthly Operating Costs
lessons.body: Once your pig farm is running, you face monthly costs that must be paid even before you sell any pigs. For a batch farrowing system with 5 sows, your monthly operating costs will be around $800 to $1,200. The biggest chunk is feed, which we'll cover in the next lesson, but for now, know that feed alone can be $500 to $700 per month. Labour is next: if you hire one full-time worker, expect to pay $100 to $200 per month, depending on your country. In many African countries, you can find reliable help for $120 per month. If you do the work yourself, that's money saved, but your time has value. Utilities: water and electricity. If you have a borehole, water is cheap, but if you buy water, budget $50 per month. Electricity for lighting and maybe a feed grinder: $30 to $50. Vet and health: even without a disease outbreak, you need routine deworming, vaccinations, and vitamins. Budget $50 to $100 per month. Transport: to buy feed, take pigs to market, or visit the vet. If you have a motorcycle, fuel and maintenance cost $50 per month. If you hire transport, it can be $100 or more. Maintenance and repairs: things breakâwater pipes, feeders, roofs. Set aside $50 per month. Miscellaneous: soap, disinfectants, tools, phone airtime for calling buyers. $30. Loan repayments: if you borrowed money to start, include that. For a $2,000 loan at 10% annual interest over 2 years, you pay about $92 per month. Total monthly operating costs: roughly $900 to $1,200. To manage these costs, keep a monthly budget book. Track every expense. At the end of each month, compare actual spending to your budget. If you overspend on feed, find out whyâmaybe you're wasting feed or your pigs are sick. Buy feed in bulk to get discounts. Share transport with neighbouring farmers. Do your own vaccinations if trained. And always pay yourself a small salary so you don't dip into operating money. Remember, you only get income when you sell pigs. In batch farrowing, sales come in cycles, so you must have enough cash to cover 2-3 months of expenses before your first batch is ready.

lessons.title: Feed: 65-75% of All Costs
lessons.body: Feed is the single biggest expense in pig farming. In Africa, feed alone takes 65 to 75 cents out of every dollar you spend. If your monthly costs are $1,000, then $650 to $750 goes to feed. That's why managing feed is the key to profit. A lactating sow with piglets eats about 5 kg of feed per day. A dry sow eats 2.5 kg. A growing pig eats 1.5 to 2 kg per day. For 5 sows and 50 piglets, you need roughly 500 kg of feed per week, or 2,000 kg per month. If commercial feed costs $0.50 per kg, that's $1,000 per month just for feed. But you can reduce this. First, mix your own feed. Buy maize, soya bean meal, fish meal, and premix in bulk. A typical pig feed recipe: 60% maize, 20% soya, 10% fish meal, 5% wheat bran, 5% premix and minerals. This can cut your cost to $0.35 per kg. That saves you $300 per month. Second, grow your own maize or cassava. If you have land, plant maize. One hectare can produce 2,000 kg of maize, worth $600. That's three months of feed for your pigs. Third, reduce waste. Use feeders that prevent spillage. Don't overfeed. A sow doesn't need unlimited feed; follow a feeding chart. Fourth, store feed properly to avoid mould and rats. Use airtight containers or raised pallets. Mouldy feed causes abortions and slow growth. Fifth, use alternative feeds like sweet potato vines, pumpkin, and kitchen waste, but only as supplementsâthey don't replace balanced feed. Sixth, buy feed ingredients during harvest when prices are low. Maize is cheapest right after harvest. Store it dry. Seventh, consider fermenting feed. Fermented feed improves digestion and reduces cost by 10-15%. To ferment, mix feed with water in a sealed container for 2-3 days. It smells like silage. Pigs love it. Finally, monitor your feed conversion ratio (FCR). FCR is how many kg of feed to produce 1 kg of pig. A good FCR is 3:1. If your FCR is 4:1, you're wasting feed. Weigh your pigs monthly to track growth. Keep records of feed bought and used. If feed is 70% of costs, a 10% saving on feed is a 7% saving on total costs. That's real money.

lessons.title: Labour and Overheads
lessons.body: Labour and overheads are the second and third biggest costs after feed. In a small pig farm in Africa, you might do all the work yourself, but as you grow, you'll need help. Labour costs include salaries, food, and housing for workers. A full-time pig caretaker in Kenya or Nigeria earns about $100 to $150 per month. In South Africa, it's $200 to $300. If you hire part-time help for cleaning and feeding, you might pay $50 per month. But labour is not just salary. You must also provide gloves, boots, and overalls. That's $20 per month. If the worker lives on the farm, you provide housing and food, which can add $50 per month. Overheads are the ongoing costs that don't change with the number of pigs. These include rent or land rates, insurance, licences, and administration. If you rent land, that's $50 to $100 per month. If you own land, you still pay land ratesâmaybe $10 per month. Insurance for pigs and buildings: $30 per month. Business licence and permits: $20 per month. Administration: phone, internet, stationery, bank charges. $30 per month. Security: a guard or fence maintenance. $40 per month. Water and electricity we covered under operating costs, but they are also overheads. Total labour and overheads for a 5-sow farm: about $300 to $500 per month. To reduce labour costs, train your workers to do multiple tasks. A good caretaker can also do minor vet work, record keeping, and feed mixing. Pay them well to avoid theft and negligence. Use family labour where possible, but be professional. For overheads, share costs with neighbours. Buy insurance as a group to get lower premiums. Use solar power to cut electricity bills. Harvest rainwater to cut water bills. Keep overheads low, but don't compromise on security or health. Remember, overheads are fixedâyou pay them whether you sell pigs or not. So in months with no sales, you still need cash. That's why you must have a reserve fund. Aim to keep 3 months of overheads in a savings account. This buffer will save your farm during disease outbreaks or market slumps.

lessons.title: Vet, Transport and Maintenance
lessons.body: These three costs are often forgotten, but they can break your budget if you don't plan for them. Vet costs include vaccinations, dewormers, antibiotics, and professional fees. In Africa, you must vaccinate against swine fever, foot and mouth, and erysipelas. A vaccine dose costs $0.50 to $1 per pig. For 5 sows and 50 piglets, that's $30 per round. You vaccinate sows twice a year and piglets once. Deworming: every 3 months, at $0.20 per pig, so $10 per round. Antibiotics for sick pigs: $20 per month on average. Vet consultation: $20 per visit, maybe twice a year. Total vet costs: about $100 to $150 per month. To reduce, learn to do your own vaccinations and deworming. Attend a training course. Buy vaccines in bulk and share with other farmers. Keep your farm clean to prevent disease. Transport costs include moving feed, pigs, and supplies. If you buy feed from town, you need a pickup or motorcycle. Fuel and maintenance: $50 to $100 per month. If you hire transport, it's $0.10 per kg per km. For 2,000 kg of feed over 20 km, that's $40 per trip. You might do 4 trips per month, so $160. To reduce, buy feed in bulk once a month. Use a bicycle or wheelbarrow for short distances. Sell pigs at the farm gate to avoid transport to market. If you must transport pigs, use a well-ventilated truck and avoid overcrowding. Maintenance costs: your buildings, fences, water pipes, and feeders need repair. A leaking roof, a broken drinker, a rusty gateâthese add up. Set aside $50 per month for maintenance. Keep a toolbox and spare parts. Fix small problems before they become big. For example, a $2 washer can save a $200 pump. Train your workers to report damage immediately. Keep a maintenance log. Total vet, transport, and maintenance: $200 to $300 per month. To manage these, include them in your monthly budget. Don't wait for an emergency. If you see a sick pig, act fastâearly treatment is cheaper. If you see a broken fence, fix it before pigs escape. These costs are controllable if you are proactive. Remember, a healthy pig is a profitable pig. A well-maintained farm has fewer disease problems. So spend wisely hereâit's an investment, not just an expense.

lessons.title: Cost Per Pig Formula
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must calculate your cost per pig. This is the total cost of producing one pig from birth to sale. The formula is: Cost per Pig = Total Costs Ã· Number of Pigs Sold. But total costs include all expenses: feed, labour, vet, transport, maintenance, overheads, and startup costs spread over time. Let's work through an example. Suppose you have 5 sows. Each sow produces 10 piglets per batch, and you have 2 batches per year. So you sell 100 pigs per year. Your annual costs: feed $9,000, labour $1,800, vet $1,200, transport $1,200, maintenance $600, overheads $2,400, startup $4,000 (spread over 5 years, so $800 per year). Total annual cost = $9,000 + $1,800 + $1,200 + $1,200 + $600 + $2,400 + $800 = $17,000. Cost per pig = $17,000 Ã· 100 = $170. So each pig costs you $170 to produce. If you sell at $250, your profit per pig is $80. Total profit = $8,000 per year. But if you sell at $150, you lose $20 per pig. That's why you must know your cost per pig. To calculate your own, follow these steps: 1) Record all expenses for a year. 2) Count all pigs sold. 3) Divide total expenses by number of pigs. 4) Compare to your selling price. If your cost per pig is too high, find where to cut. Maybe feed is too expensiveâmix your own. Maybe labour is highâdo more yourself. Maybe you have too many pig deathsâimprove health. Also calculate cost per kg. If a pig weighs 80 kg and costs $170, then cost per kg is $2.13. If market price is $2.50 per kg, you profit $0.37 per kg. To reduce cost per pig, increase productivity. A sow that gives 12 piglets instead of 10 spreads your fixed costs over more pigs. Improve feed conversion. Reduce mortality. Sell at the right weightâpigs gain weight cheaply up to 80 kg, then it gets expensive. Weigh your pigs monthly to track. Use a simple notebook or a smartphone app like Farmbrite. Update your costs weekly. Review your cost per pig every batch. This number is your compass. Without it, you are farming blind. With it, you can make smart decisions and grow your profit.

quiz.q: What is the biggest startup cost for a small pig farm?
quiz.explanation: Housing, especially a concrete shed, is typically the largest single startup expense.

quiz.q: How much does a basic farrowing crate cost?
quiz.explanation: A basic farrowing crate costs between $80 and $120 each.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce startup costs?
options: B) Start with 2 sows instead of 5
D) Borrow money at high interest
quiz.explanation: Starting smaller with fewer sows reduces initial investment and risk.

quiz.q: What percentage of monthly operating costs is typically feed?
quiz.explanation: Feed accounts for 65-75% of all costs in pig farming.

quiz.q: Which of these is a monthly operating cost?
quiz.explanation: Labour is a recurring monthly expense, while the others are startup costs.

quiz.q: How much should you budget for water and electricity per month for 5 sows?
quiz.explanation: Water and electricity typically cost $80-$100 per month for a small farm.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a monthly budget book?
options: A) To show off to neighbours
B) To track expenses and avoid overspending
C) To apply for a loan
quiz.explanation: Tracking expenses helps you identify waste and stay within budget.

quiz.q: What is the biggest cost in pig farming?
quiz.explanation: Feed is the single largest expense, taking 65-75% of total costs.

quiz.q: How much feed does a lactating sow eat per day?
quiz.explanation: A lactating sow with piglets eats about 5 kg of feed per day.

quiz.q: What is a typical pig feed recipe?
options: A) 60% maize, 20% soya, 10% fish meal, 5% wheat bran, 5% premix
quiz.explanation: This balanced recipe is commonly used to reduce feed costs while meeting nutritional needs.

quiz.q: How can you reduce feed costs?
options: C) Feed more to grow faster
D) Store feed in open bags
quiz.explanation: Mixing your own feed from bulk ingredients can significantly lower cost per kg.

quiz.q: What is a good feed conversion ratio (FCR) for pigs?
quiz.explanation: A good FCR is around 3:1, meaning 3 kg of feed to produce 1 kg of pig.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of fermenting feed?
options: A) It makes feed last longer
B) It improves digestion and reduces cost
C) It makes pigs grow slower
quiz.explanation: Fermented feed improves digestion and can reduce feed cost by 10-15%.

quiz.q: What is the typical monthly salary for a full-time pig caretaker in Kenya or Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: A full-time caretaker in these countries earns about $100-$150 per month.

quiz.q: Which of these is an overhead cost?
quiz.explanation: Land rates are a fixed overhead cost that must be paid regardless of production.

quiz.q: How can you reduce labour costs?
options: B) Train workers to do multiple tasks
quiz.explanation: Multi-skilled workers can handle feeding, cleaning, and minor vet work, reducing the need for extra staff.

quiz.q: Why should you keep 3 months of overheads in savings?
options: B) To cover fixed costs during no-sales periods
C) To pay for a holiday
quiz.explanation: A reserve fund ensures you can pay overheads even when you have no income from pig sales.

quiz.q: What is a common vet cost for a small pig farm?
quiz.explanation: Vet costs, including vaccinations and deworming, average $100-$150 per month.

quiz.q: How can you reduce vet costs?
options: B) Learn to do your own vaccinations
quiz.explanation: Training to administer vaccines and dewormers yourself saves on professional fees.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce transport costs?
options: A) Buy feed in small quantities
B) Buy feed in bulk once a month
quiz.explanation: Buying in bulk reduces the number of trips and lowers transport costs.

quiz.q: Why is maintenance important?
options: B) It prevents small problems from becoming big expenses
D) It only applies to buildings
quiz.explanation: Regular maintenance, like fixing a leaking roof, avoids costly repairs later.

quiz.q: What is the formula for cost per pig?
options: A) Total Costs Ã Number of Pigs
B) Total Costs Ã· Number of Pigs Sold
C) Number of Pigs Ã· Total Costs
quiz.explanation: Cost per pig is calculated by dividing total costs by the number of pigs sold.

quiz.q: If total annual costs are $17,000 and you sell 100 pigs, what is your cost per pig?
If your cost per pig is $170 and you sell at $250, what is your profit per pig?
quiz.explanation: $250 - $170 = $80 profit per pig.

quiz.q: Why should you sell pigs at around 80 kg?
options: B) Feed conversion gets worse after 80 kg
quiz.explanation: After 80 kg, pigs require more feed per kg of gain, reducing profitability.

quiz.q: What tool can help you track costs per pig?
options: A) A smartphone app like Farmbrite
quiz.explanation: Farmbrite and similar apps help record and calculate costs easily.

quiz.q: How can you reduce cost per pig?
quiz.explanation: More piglets per sow spreads fixed costs over more pigs, lowering cost per pig.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of knowing your cost per pig?
options: B) You can set a profitable selling price
C) You can avoid record keeping
D) You can ignore market prices
quiz.explanation: Knowing your cost per pig helps you determine the minimum price needed to make a profit.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in calculating cost per pig?
options: B) Forgetting to include startup costs
quiz.explanation: Startup costs must be spread over the years they benefit, or your cost per pig will be understated.

quiz.q: What should you do if your cost per pig is higher than the market price?
options: B) Find ways to cut costs or increase productivity
quiz.explanation: You must either reduce costs (e.g., mix feed) or improve productivity (e.g., more piglets per sow) to become profitable.
